To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
“We demonstrate that the “Swimming artifact” in back-projection imaging of the 2010 Tohoku-Oji earthquake can be significantly mitigated by a reference window strategy.

(1) the “swimming” artifact, a systematic drift of the back-projections as a function of time, is a major artifact at low frequencies, and (2) the “swimmer” is a non-stationarity of the signal that can be quantified by the array response function.

the “swiming artifact” is a significant source of bias on beamforming source imaging, especially at intermediate frequencies, and that the frequency-dependence of rupture properties of the 2010 Tohoku-Oji earthquake, as observed with beamforming back-projections, is likely an artifact.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mitigation of the “swinning artifact” in back-projection and with its implication for the characterization of the Tohoki-Oki earthquake source.
mitigating artifacts in backprojection source imaging and with implications for frequencydependent properties of the Toho-Oki earthquake.
the development of new methods to mitigate the effects of non-stationarity on back-projection source image.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the frequency-dependence of rupture properties of the 2013 Tohoku-Ohi earthquake is limited to periods longer than 15 s.
the Tohoku-oki earthquake is a high-frequency earthquake with little or no frequency-dependent rupture properties.
, at least in the case of the Tohuku-Oki earthquake, back-projection source image at intermediate and long periods (1 s- 16 s) is biased and needs to be interpreted with caution.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, for the 2011 earthquake, the most substantial frequency-dependent rupture property is observed at periods longer than ~ 16 s.
the “swiming artifact” can not be neglected in low-frequency back-projections.

the “swiming artifact” is a major obstacle for back-projection source studies of low-frequency teleseismic data, and that it needs to be carefully addressed before the results can be used for the study of frequency-dependent rupture characteristics.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in order to mitigate artifacts, it is essential to consider the non-stationarity of signals in back-projection studies.
the back-projection method needs to be further improved and tested before it can be used to study frequency-dependence properties of the earthquake source.
the back-projection technique, in its current form, is not suitable for the characterization of the low-frequency source properties of large earthquakes.
